0.0.n: An affectionate, familiar way to refer to an older sister; お adds warmth here.

0.1.n: Marks the person the speaker will meet; 会う uses に for this.

0.2.n: The shortened form of 会う used before に行く to express the purpose of going.

0.3.n: Follows 会い to mark the purpose of going.

0.4.n: The plain form expresses a future plan here, not an action happening right now.

0.5.n: Adds emphasis as the speaker announces the plan to the listener.

1.0.n: A noun for the place someone intends to reach.

1.1.n: Marks 目的地 as the topic: the sentence tells us where the destination is.

1.2.n: The Japanese name of the French capital, written in katakana.

2.0.n: An energetic call to begin an action or set off.

2.2.n: A country name written in katakana; here it names the place the speaker urges heading toward.

3.0.n: With rising intonation, this short reaction shows surprise or confusion.

3.2.n: The country name is repeated as a question to show disbelief or seek confirmation.

4.0.n: The city name is brought up again to correct the mistaken country.

4.1.n: Marks パリ as the topic of the correction.

4.2.n: The Japanese name of the country where Paris is located.

4.3.n: Part of the regional ending ぞな, which gives the correction an assertive, folksy tone.

4.4.n: Completes the regional ending ぞな; read the two together rather than as separate standard endings.

0.lit: Big sister—with—see—in order to—go—I tell you!
0.tip: The two に have different jobs: one marks whom you meet, the other marks why you go.

1.tip: Casual exclamations can omit だ, the word that would explicitly express is.

2.tip: いざ makes this a spirited call to set off, even without a verb like go.

3.tip: Repeating a word with rising intonation can express surprise without forming a full question.

4.tip: ぞな is a regional sentence ending, giving this correction a folksy flavor rather than standard textbook phrasing.
